CARES Architecture

Status: proposed architecture; not implemented. This document records a target architecture, not evidence that CARES services, infrastructure, or controls exist. The current repository contains only small in-memory Python prototypes; see PROJECT_STATUS.md.

Architectural principles

  • Python is the primary language for the backend.
  • PostgreSQL is the required primary relational database; there is no database integration in the current code.
  • MELIRA uses customer-selected external AI SaaS providers. CARES does not require local GPU resources, must not silently fail over to another provider, and must enforce privacy policy before any provider request.
  • One unique monitored device is one licensed asset, independent of device type and number of collection sources.
  • Begin as a modular monolith with deployable worker processes. Split services only when measured scale, availability, or ownership needs justify the operational cost.
  • Enforce tenant authorization at API/service and database boundaries. A prompt or UI filter is not authorization. Database access must rely on protected, verifier-written, transaction-bound verified tenant context; custom PostgreSQL GUCs (for example SET app.tenant_id) are not authentication or authorization sources and may be used only for non-authoritative diagnostics if approved. See SECURITY_ARCHITECTURE.md and ARCHITECTURE_DECISION_PACKAGE_FINAL_CORRECTIONS.md.
  • Keep core monitoring and detection independent of MELIRA.

Proposed system boundary

The initial product is a web control plane and data plane backed by PostgreSQL. The Dashboard calls the CARES API. Agents and integrations send authenticated data to ingestion endpoints. Processing is separated from synchronous API requests using a transactional outbox and a separately run worker. Both may initially be packaged from one Python codebase and share the same database, but have distinct responsibilities and runtime limits.

The architecture deliberately does not require a separate broker, cache, search engine, analytics database, or Kubernetes cluster for an initial deployment. Those are scale-driven options, not prerequisites.

Asset registration is a tenant-scoped identity-resolution transaction, not a count of incoming agents or integrations. CARES assigns an immutable canonical asset UUID and resolves identity through stable source-device bindings (asset_data_source / source_device_key_id) and versioned fingerprint aliases (source_device_fingerprint_alias) rather than treating a fingerprint as permanent binding identity. CARES records source-specific identity claims with provenance and only automatically attaches a source on a unique authoritative match. Weak or conflicting identifiers create a pending resolution rather than an automatic merge. The transaction must establish verified tenant context, apply deterministic locking/post-lock rechecks, persist required idempotency/licensing/audit/outbox records atomically as designed, and change licensed usage only according to approved state-to-counter policy. See DATA_ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/adr/0006-atomic-per-tenant-asset-licensing.md for reconciled semantics (proposed, NOT IMPLEMENTED/NOT TESTED).

The proposed initial load profile is an assumption, not measured capacity: 10 tenants, 5,000 active assets, 25 events/second sustained, and a 100 events/second five-minute burst, with a 1 KiB average event and 256 KiB maximum event. PostgreSQL is the initial event store and outbox; no broker or analytical database is required at that profile. Performance targets and infrastructure decision gates are documented in DATA_ARCHITECTURE.md and must be validated against a fixed benchmark environment before being treated as commitments.

The external SaaS link is optional. If AI is disabled, unconfigured, policy-blocked, or unavailable, core ingestion, detection, incident handling, and reporting continue without it. No provider failover is implicit.

Data ingestion and processing flow

flowchart TD
  SRC["Agent / integration"] --> AUTH["Authenticate source; resolve tenant and source identity"]
  AUTH --> LIMIT["Validate schema, size, rate and tenant technical quota"]
  LIMIT --> ASSET["Resolve namespaced identity claims and source binding"]
  ASSET -->|unique authoritative match| DEDUPE["Attach source to existing tenant asset"]
  ASSET -->|trusted new identity| QUOTA{"Lock tenant quota; recheck aliases"}
  ASSET -->|ambiguous, weak-only, or conflict| PENDING["Pending identity review; no normal analysis"]
  QUOTA -->|quota available| CREATE["Create one canonical asset + source + history"]
  QUOTA -->|quota full| REJECT["Reject/quarantine registration; record reason"]
  DEDUPE --> EVENT["Write idempotency receipt, event and outbox atomically"]
  CREATE --> EVENT
  EVENT --> WORK["Bounded worker"]
  WORK --> PARSE["Parse and validate"]
  PARSE --> NORMAL["Normalize / enrich"]
  NORMAL --> CORR["Correlate and detect"]
  CORR --> ALERT["Persist alert / case updates"]
  ALERT --> REPORT["Tenant-scoped API and reporting"]
  REJECT --> AUDIT["Audit and usage record"]
  PENDING --> REVIEW["Authorized merge / split / bind review"]
  REVIEW -->|resolved; quota checked atomically| EVENT
  EVENT --> AUDIT

Identity resolution is deliberately a separate, explicit stage. Source-local identifiers are namespaced; exact, unique authoritative identifiers may be matched deterministically. Stable source-device bindings and versioned fingerprint aliases must be distinguished (fingerprints/aliases are not permanent binding identity), and overlap/rotation/collision/migration must not create duplicate assets, bindings, aliases, or licensed usage. IP addresses and hostnames are observations and weak correlation attributes only. A source with ambiguous identity is held from normal customer analysis pending authorized review per approved policy; it is not automatically billed as another confirmed device or merged into a candidate. Merge/split operations preserve canonical IDs, binding/alias/event lineage, usage/licensing history, and audit records under atomic, idempotent, tenant-isolated transactions (proposed). The precise confidence classification, quarantine defaults, pending/reservation/accounting policy, and removal grace policy remain proposals requiring owner approval. If two collection sources cannot establish that they refer to the same device, the product must not silently claim reliable deduplication.

  INTERNET["Internet / customer networks"] --> WAF["Managed edge: TLS, rate limits, request limits"]

    API
    ING
    WORK

  end

Initial development and small deployments may use a single-host container composition, with PostgreSQL isolated and backed up. A production SaaS deployment should use managed PostgreSQL, private networking, controlled egress, external secret management, and independently scalable API/worker processes. These are deployment targets, not current services. Kubernetes is deferred until a concrete availability/scale requirement outweighs its operational cost.

MELIRA provider integration architecture

flowchart LR
  USER["Authorized analyst"] --> API["CARES API"]
  API --> AUTH["Tenant-scoped authorization + tool allow-list"]
  AUTH --> CONTEXT["Fetch only allowed evidence"]
  CONTEXT --> GATE["Consent + privacy policy gate"]
  GATE --> CLASS["Classify, minimize, redact"]
  CLASS --> CHOICE{"Explicitly configured provider / region"}
  CHOICE -->|none / disabled| STOP["Return unavailable; no transmission"]
  CHOICE -->|selected| TERMS["Check provider region, retention, training terms"]
  TERMS --> BUDGET["Preflight tenant request/token/spend budget"]
  TERMS -->|unknown or denied| DENY["No provider request; audit policy decision"]
  BUDGET -->|exhausted| DENY
  BUDGET -->|allowed| ENDPOINT["Validate HTTPS destination + egress policy"]
  ENDPOINT --> ADAPTER["Provider-specific adapter"]
  VAULT["Secret manager / encrypted secret store"] --> ADAPTER
  ADAPTER -->|TLS, fixed/validated endpoint| SaaS["Selected external SaaS"]
  SaaS --> ADAPTER
  ADAPTER --> OUTPUT["Validate response; cite CARES evidence IDs"]
  OUTPUT --> API
  DENY --> API
  STOP --> API
  DENY -. no prompt content in audit .-> AUDIT["Protected request audit"]
  OUTPUT -. outcome and usage metadata .-> AUDIT

The provider adapter must not own tenant authorization or decide which records are visible. The customer explicitly selects one enabled provider/model/region for each request; an absent selection, disabled provider, policy denial, provider error, or exhausted budget returns a clear unavailable/blocked/error result. There is no implicit provider or model failover, and no local inference/GPU path.

Before any provider call, CARES authorizes the user and tool independently of the model, fetches only tenant-authorized evidence, classifies it, obtains the required customer consent/policy, minimizes and sanitizes data, checks residency/retention/training terms and the tenant usage budget, and records an audit event. Credentials are referenced from a secret manager, are never returned to the UI or logged, and have explicit rotation/revocation. Provider endpoints are allow-listed HTTPS destinations; custom endpoints are disabled unless platform policy validates their hostname, resolved IPs, redirects, and egress route to prevent SSRF and DNS rebinding. Provider responses and tool requests are untrusted; every tool action is independently authorized, with human approval for high-impact actions.

The initially supported vendor list, consent granularity, permitted data-classification matrix, residency regions, provider retention/training requirements, credential ownership model, and spend ceilings are unresolved decisions. See SECURITY_ARCHITECTURE.md and ADR 0004.

CARES Agent communication architecture

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant Admin as Authorized installer workflow
  participant API as Enrollment service
  participant CA as CARES certificate authority / issuer
  participant Agent as CARES Agent
  participant Ingest as Ingestion API
  participant DB as PostgreSQL

  Admin->>API: Request short-lived, single-use enrollment token
  API->>DB: Verify tenant quota and record issuance
  API-->>Admin: Installer/configuration without reusable tenant secret
  Agent->>API: Present token over TLS
  API->>DB: Atomically consume token; register agent source and device
  API->>CA: Issue unique device certificate (proposed)
  CA-->>Agent: Certificate + trust material
  Agent->>Ingest: TLS/mTLS heartbeat and sequenced event batch
  Ingest->>DB: Validate identity, tenant binding, limits; persist + outbox
  Ingest-->>Agent: Acknowledged sequence range
  Note over Agent: Buffer bounded events offline; retry with backoff and deduplication key
  Agent->>Ingest: Resume from acknowledged sequence after reconnect

Agent commands, removal, and updates need signed, expiring, replay-resistant envelopes and explicit authorization. This sequence is a target protocol only; no agent, enrollment endpoint, certificate authority, or command channel exists in the repository.

Evolution and decision gates

Keep module boundaries explicit: identity/access, tenant administration, asset/licensing, ingestion, event processing, detection, case management, integrations, reporting, and AI. A worker is a process boundary, not a separately operated microservice by default.

Evaluate partitioning, an event broker, dedicated search/analytics stores, and service extraction only after measured workload and service objectives show PostgreSQL and the modular worker design are insufficient. Any change must preserve tenant scope, auditability, asset licensing semantics, and AI optionality.
